https://www.theguardian.com/science/ng-i.text: Prague Castle is silhouetted against a partial solar eclipse Photograph: Martin Divíšek/EPA View image in fullscreen Prague Castle is silhouetted against a partial solar eclipse Photograph: Martin Divíšek/EPA Solar eclipses Cruise ships, quiet towns and an all-day festival: millions flock to eclipse viewing spots across Europe Beginning in Russia’s remote Arctic north, the eclipse traced an arc over much of western Europe – with the best views in Spain, Iceland and Greenland Ashifa Kassam in Madrid, Miranda Bryant and Chris Michael in London Wed 12 Aug 2026 15.56 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 17.10 EDT Share It was a moment of awe shared by millions across Europe: an eclipse that blocked out the sun, plunging parts of the continent into a daytime darkness in which temperatures dropped and birds suddenly went quiet. Wednesday’s eclipse began in Russia’s remote Arctic north, going on to trace an arc over much of western Europe. From the UK to northern Italy, tens of millions of people turned to the sky as the light of the setting sun was almost completely blocked out. The most sought-after experiences were in Greenland, Iceland and Spain along with a small strip of Portugal. It was in parts of these countries that totality – referring to when the moon completely covers the sun’s light – was on offer, drawing millions of local people and thousands of tourists from across the globe into the path of the eclipse. “It was one of the most beautiful things I’ve ever seen in my life,” Sara García Alonso, a reserve astronaut for the European Space Agency, told broadcaster RTVE. “It gave me goosebumps.” Standing next to her, the astronaut Pablo Álvarez Fernández nodded in agreement: “It had been described to me so many times, but it was much more beautiful than what I had expected.” In Iceland, people flocked by air, land and sea to take in the country’s first total solar eclipse in 72 years. Amid concerns that clouds would block the view, a record 31 cruise ships plied the waters off the western part of the country, hoping to secure a top view for about 53,000 passengers and crew. View image in fullscreen The sun during a partial solar eclipse and partially obscured by clouds, the International Space Station silhouetted as it transits at roughly five miles per second. Photograph: Nasa Handout/EPA View image in fullscreen People gather to observe the total solar eclipse, as clouds cover the sky, in Reykjavik Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters View image in fullscreen Passengers on board the Ambassador cruise ship Ambition watching the start of the total solar eclipse off the coast of Greenland Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PA The eclipse-themed activities included a day-long music festival hosted by the Icelandic artist Björk in Víðistaðatún park, offering a DJ-curated backdrop as people took in the eclipse. The 10-hour set list included two minutes set aside for totality, the artist said on social media, while the festival website noted that every ticket included a pair of approved solar eclipse glasses. Those watching from Iceland included the US space agency, Nasa, which followed the moon’s shadow using a high-altitude WB-57 aircraft while Nasa-funded teams launched balloons to study the atmospheric impact of the sudden darkness and cooling. View image in fullscreen A WB-57 Canberra aircraft is pictured during a media visit ahead of a Nasa-supported mission Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters View image in fullscreen Cary Klemm, sensor equipment operator, and pilot John Gustine of Nasa’s Johnson Space Centre pose in front of a WB-57 Canberra aircraft Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters View image in fullscreen A WB-57 Canberra aircraft Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters View image in fullscreen A gyroscopic sensor system aboard a WB-57 Canberra aircraft Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters In Spain, where some of the best views of the total eclipse were expected, the hours leading up to the celestial alignment were filled with frenzied debate about weather forecasts and where best to watch the phenomenon. More than 450,000 tourists had arrived in the country from as far as Canada and Australia, crisscrossing Spain by train, bus and caravan to stake out the perfect viewing spot. View image in fullscreen The sun’s corona glows as the moon completely blocks the sun during the totality phase of the total solar eclipse as seen from San Asensio, La Rioja region, Spain Photograph: Ander Gillenea/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen People wait for a solar eclipse at the beach in A Coruña, Spain Photograph: Lavandeira/EPA View image in fullscreen A beachgoer wearing special eclipse glasses looks up during the beginning phase of a solar eclipse at Puerto de Sagunto beach near Valencia, Spain Photograph: Alberto Saiz/AP View image in fullscreen The sun’s corona glows as the moon completely blocks the sun during the totality phase of the total solar eclipse as seen from Arenal beach in Llucmajor, on the Balearic island of Mallorca Photograph: Jaime Reina/AFP/Getty Images “Our car was cancelled,” one woman, who had travelled from Brazil with her sister to take in the eclipse, said on social media. After her appeals to hitch a ride to their chosen site were met with no response, they took matters into their own hands. “So we took a three-hour bus, a 20-minute taxi and two-hour hike. Arrived at the location!” About 10,000 metres above sea level, the Spanish airline Iberia livestreamed the moment when the sun, moon and Earth aligned from a special charter flight. “Some flights take us to new destinations. Others allow us to see the world from a different perspective,” the airline said as it announced the charter flight. Spanish officials estimated that as many as 6 million people were expected to flock to the path of the eclipse, which stretched about 124 miles (200km) from A Coruña in Spain’s north-west to the Mediterranean island of Mallorca. On Wednesday, just hours before the eclipse, officials reported traffic jams on the major thoroughfares out of Madrid and Barcelona. Others took their chances in the cities. In Madrid’s Parque del Oeste, hundreds gathered in hopes of catching a good view of the eclipse, cheering as they watched the moon cover the sun – plunging the park into darkness – and gasping as the outer corona left a glowing halo around the moon. Just over a minute later, when daylight returned to the park, the crowd burst into raucous cheers. It was, in the words of César González, an astronomer and science communicator at the Madrid Planetarium, “a spectacular experience”. He had left Madrid early in the morning to set himself up in a field in northern Spain to watch the eclipse. “Until one goes and experiences it, there’s no way to explain what it is to see an eclipse.” View image in fullscreen Mario Garrido, a member of the Los Taraos amateur astrophotography group, waits to shoot a total solar eclipse in Berlanga de Duero, central Spain Photograph: Bernat Armangué/AP View image in fullscreen The moon completely covers the sun during a total solar eclipse as seen from the Javalambre Astrophysical Observatory in Arcos de las Salinas, near Teruel, Spain Photograph: Christian Hartmann/Reuters View image in fullscreen Artists use self-made artefacts to observe a solar eclipse before totality near the small village of Castell de Cabres, Spain Photograph: Eva Manez/Reuters View image in fullscreen A composite image of seven separate photographs taken with a single fixed camera shows stages of a solar eclipse before, during and after totality, as seen from Arija, Spain Photograph: Borja Suárez/Reuters He was able, however, to explain the impact. “In broad daylight, all of a sudden the light dims to a point where you can see the brightest stars in the sky. When totality starts, the temperature drops several degrees. If you’re in a field and surrounded by animals, their behaviour often changes. The birds stop singing because they think it’s nightfall. And all of this lasts for a few minutes – in this case around 1 minute and 45 seconds.” In Spain, most eclipse watchers were heading to rural areas, filling often quiet villages and towns clogged with skygazing tourists. The eclipse had helped put some parts of “empty Spain” on the map; this week people linked to Nasa turn up in northern Spain’s Villalibado to set up a live broadcast for millions of people around the world, breathing new life into a municipality whose last two residents left in 1998. Throughout human history, eclipses have sparked amazement, fear and reverence. In villages and cities across Europe, the eclipse forged ad hoc communities, as people came together to witness one of nature’s great wonders. In Camberwell, south London, an impromptu crowd of all ages gathered in Brunswick Park to experiment with different methods of seeing the eclipse, which reached 92% totality. Some held up colanders, others a spatula with holes, still others makeshift pinhole cameras made of old candy boxes. Ludmila, a Ukrainian woman in her 70s, said she had worked at an observatory in Crimea for 30 years. “What a surprise to find an actual refractor,” she said, pointing to a telescope with a solar filter taped on the end brought out by a resident. “It’s like a wonderful gift.” Later, as the eclipse passed its zenith and the sun began to set for real, dozens of neighbours who had never previously spoken to each other stayed on picnic blankets to drink beer and swap photos. https://tribune.com.pk/story/2622294/gov.text: Home Business Govt rejects consultant report on tight gas Second evaluation confirms presence of tight gas reserves in Rehman-8 ST-3 well The government has rejected findings of the first international consultant and has approved the presence of tight gas in an exploration field operated by Polish Oil and Gas Company. The consultant hired by the director general petroleum concessions (DGPC) declared that the gas field had no tight gas reserves. But the DG hired a second consultant, who confirmed that the gas found by the Polish firm was tight gas, which raised doubts about the certification. Sources told The Express Tribune that the case was tabled in a recent meeting of the Economic Coordination Committee (ECC), where it was highlighted that Polish Oil and Gas Company (POGC) had requested for approval of re-evaluation and re-certification of tight gas reserves in Rehman-8 ST-3 well, located in Rehman Development and Production Lease, in accordance with Clause 5(h) of the Tight Gas (E&P) Policy, 2011. The Ministry of Energy (Petroleum Division) recalled that drilling on Rehman-8 ST-3 well started on August 5, 2021 and it reached a total depth of 2,845 metres on May 2, 2023. Based on the initial production performance and reservoir characteristics, POGC requested the declaration of the well as a tight gas reservoir under the 2011 policy. Accordingly, after competitive bidding, RPS was engaged as a third-party consultant to certify the reservoir. However, the report submitted by RPS was not accepted and declined vide letter dated October 23, 2024. POGC was also informed that the reservoir and the associated deposits would be considered conventional reserves. The Petroleum Division told the meeting that subsequently, upon request from POGC, a re-evaluation of Rehman-8 ST-3 well was carried out by another internationally reputed third-party consultant, namely IPR International, in accordance with Clause 5(h) of the Tight Gas (E&P) Policy, 2011. The consultant concluded that the gas-bearing reservoir in Rehman-8 ST-3 qualified as tight gas under the 2011 policy. "The reservoir cannot be produced economically using conventional production and completion techniques. It can be commercially exploited using unconventional techniques, such as high-performance perforation coupled with semi-massive hydraulic fracturing," it said. Based on a detailed evaluation, IPR International certified that the reservoir permeability was approximately 0.91 milli-Darcy, which was below the threshold of 1.0 milli-Darcy prescribed under the Tight Gas Policy, 2011, thereby qualifying as tight gas deposits. The Petroleum Division revealed that a technical team of the director general petroleum concessions raised certain observations about the consultant's recommendations. In response, the consultant provided its response and justifications, which were part of the report. It is pertinent to highlight that the certification of tight gas reserves is required under the 2011 policy from an independent third-party consultant. In the present case, a renowned consultant confirmed the tight nature of the reservoir, leaving limited regulatory discretion to disregard such a certification. The Petroleum Division pointed out that in the wake of Supreme Court's judgement in the Mustafa Impex case, the term "government" was construed as the federal cabinet, comprising the prime minister and federal ministers; therefore, the cabinet's approval was required for the declaration of Rehman-8 ST-3 as a tight gas well. In light of the foregoing, the Petroleum Division solicited approval of the ECC, which considered a summary titled "Tight Gas Reserves and Reservoir Re-Certification in Respect of Rehman-8 ST-3 under Tight Gas (Exploration & Production) Policy, 2011", and approved the proposal. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text: Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog. A US federal judge has blocked the Trump administration from enforcing a new executive order limiting who qualifies for birthright citizenship. The move thwarts President Donald Trump’s latest attempt to restrict the constitutional right, which comes after the US supreme court rejected his previous effort, AFP reported. US district judge Deborah Boardman of Maryland issued a preliminary injunction following an appeal by rights groups who challenged Trump’s executive order from 6 August targeting what he termed “birth tourism”. “The supreme court has spoken: Children in the certified class are ’citizens at birth’,” Boardman wrote in her 35-page ruling, adding the president’s August order “is almost certainly unconstitutional”. “When it comes to attacking birthright citizenship, the Trump administration has lost before this court, lost before the supreme court, and lost again today,” said Shana Khader, legal director at We Are CASA, a Maryl

https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-unvei.text: BRUSSELS — Brussels on Monday unveiled an environmental rating scheme for data centers that power artificial intelligence, a move the EU's energy chief described as the first step in pressuring tech giants into aligning with the continent’s climate efforts. The new rules , which will apply from August 2027, oblige big data centers to display a label grading them on their energy efficiency, water usage and clean power uptake on a scale of A to G, much like the EU's influential appliances ranking . “This will add a lot of transparency and hopefully provide the incentives for these data centers to be as sustainable as possible,” said Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen in an interview with POLITICO ahead of the label's presentation. Advertisement Advertisement The new label is optional for smaller data centers, “but later we are also going to introduce minimum performance standards which, of course, will put more pressure on those who may not voluntarily wish to be as sustainable as we want them to,” he added. While Australia and Singapore already have schemes rating the energy efficiency of data centers, the Commission's new label would be the most comprehensive worldwide — asking tech companies to be transparent not only about their power use but also their impact on the local and global environment via information on how much water they consume, how clean their electricity is, whether they reuse the heat they generate and more. The EU executive's performance standards, which the Commission wants to present in spring 2027, are expected to tighten the screws by setting mandatory sustainability thresholds for newly built or retrofitted data centers. Those two initiatives are an attempt at ensuring the European Union can compete in the artificial intelligence race without sacrificing its commitment to climate neutrality in 2050, Jørgensen said. “We need to deal with this in a way that data centers in the future are not something that will hurt our energy systems, and thereby our competitiveness and capabilities of decarbonizing and making sure we have security of supply for our citizens,” he said. “If we do not make sure that these big power consumers are indeed in line with our overall objectives… then they will risk undermining our ability to live up to our own targets,” Jørgensen warned. Data centers are already hoovering up 2.5% of the bloc’s electricity use, a share expected to double in the coming years, he noted. “We’re looking at a huge change.” Advertisement Advertisement Monday's announcement is a delegated regulation, meaning that it can take effect without the input of EU governments and the European Parliament. The two institutions have two months to object to the regulation, however. The label will be generated automatically each year from figures companies are already required to report under the bloc's energy efficiency rules, though an accompanying Commission report acknowledges that compliance with those rules is low: Only 36% of sites in the EU disclose required data. Go green, get popular Data center operators have lobbied against the Commission's plans. The European Data Center Association in April warned that the requirements would kill investment and in June insisted that the bloc must prioritize AI ambitions over its climate goals. Earlier this year, a Commission document seen by POLITICO indicated that around 20 percent of Europe’s data centers could land at the bottom of the new rating scheme. But Jørgensen urged tech companies to view EU efforts to regulate their environmental impact as an "opportunity" that could help them win over a skeptical public. In the United States, a backlash is mounting against AI infrastructure, in part over its voracious appetite for energy and water. Similar protests are starting to emerge in Europe. Advertisement Advertisement “We do see some places where public opinion is maybe turning a little bit against these data centers, we've seen it in some places in Europe and we see it even more so in the United States of America,” said Jørgensen. “So I firmly believe that it's also in the interest of the data centers to be able to show how sustainable they are.” But he indicated that the EU would not impose bloc-wide rules requiring data center operators to provide their own clean energy, something his Commission colleague Teresa Ribera advocated for in a recent interview with POLITICO. “This will always be a national decision,” he said. Still, government efforts such as Spain’s recent move toward forcing data centers to provide a share of their own renewable power are “a part of the solution in many places, because the consumption of these data centers will be so big,” he added. Overall, Jørgensen said, the EU wants to avoid developments such as in the U.S., where data centers are increasing the demand for polluting fossil fuels. “My overall message to the Big Tech sector is: We want AI, of course, we want data centers, we want Europe to be a place for investments, but it's in the interest of them and of the European Union that we do it in a way that is sustainable,” he said. “And we will be setting demands for them.” Advertisement Advertisement
